title: Start with curiosity.
text: Let the patient tell you what's bothering them in their own words.
narration: An opening question sets the tone for the encounter. Giving the patient room to describe their concern helps you understand their story before exploring the details.

title: Organize the patient's story
text: OLD CARTS is a checklist for describing a symptom. It helps you gather the details and turn the patient's story into a clear clinical summary.
narration: A patient's story gives us a starting point. OLD CARTS helps us gather the details we need to describe that story clearly. Explore the framework before you try your own summary.

title: When did it begin?
text: Onset tells us when a symptom began. Keep the starting point specific.
narration: The start of a symptom and the length of each episode answer different questions. First, notice how the patient's description helps us describe the onset more precisely.

title: How long does it last?
text: Duration tells us how long an episode lasts. Keep this separate from onset and the pattern over time.
narration: Now consider each episode on its own. The length of an episode is different from when the symptom first started or its pattern over the day.

title: Where does it occur?
text: Location identifies where the symptom occurs. Radiation describes whether it travels elsewhere.
narration: Where pain occurs and whether it travels are separate details. Compare the location with the absence of radiation, and keep both in your symptom summary.

title: Describe the symptom
text: Character describes how a symptom feels. Pleuritic pain is related to breathing.
narration: Listen for the patient's description before choosing clinical terms. Sharp describes the character, while pleuritic connects the pain to breathing. Notice how both preserve the meaning of the patient's words.

title: What changes the symptom?
text: Aggravating and alleviating factors describe what makes the symptom worse or better.
narration: Keep the feeling of pain separate from what changes it. Explore what makes the pain worse and what, if anything, helps. The absence of relief is also useful information.

title: Notice the pattern
text: Temporal factors describe the pattern over time. Duration is the length of an episode.
narration: Keep the pattern over time separate from the length of each episode. Notice how coming and going, or being worse at a particular time, adds a different kind of timing information.

title: How intense is it?
text: Severity describes intensity. Keep the patient's own rating in your summary.
narration: Ask the patient to describe the intensity in their own terms. A rating gives us a shared reference point while keeping their experience at the center of the description.

title: Patient words to clinical qualifiers
text: Listen first, then choose a precise qualifier that preserves the patient's meaning. In practice, include all eight OLD CARTS categories. Short labeled phrases are enough.
narration: A useful clinical qualifier keeps the patient's meaning intact. Compare the patient's description with sharp and pleuritic, then use the same approach when you organize Mr. Jones's facts.

title: Organize information with SOAP
accessibleDescription: Organize information with SOAP
text: SOAP means Subjective, Objective, Assessment, and Plan. It separates the information you gather from your interpretation and next steps.
narration: A clear structure helps your listener follow your thinking. As you explore SOAP, ask whether each detail is a report, a finding, an interpretation, or an action.

title: Subjective: the patient's report
accessibleDescription: Subjective: the patient's report
text: Subjective includes symptoms and history reported by the patient. Mr. Jones describes sharp pain that worsens with inspiration.
narration: Start by listening to the patient's experience. Even a precise pain rating is subjective when the patient reports it; a number alone does not make information objective.

title: Objective: observed findings
accessibleDescription: Objective: observed findings
text: Objective includes what you observe or measure. Mr. Jones's localized lung crackles are an examination finding.
narration: Now separate what you found from what you were told. The source reports stable vital signs without numbers, so keep that wording rather than inventing measurements.

title: Assessment: interpret the evidence
text: Assessment connects the findings to your clinical judgment. Explain which possibilities the evidence supports and what remains uncertain.
narration: Your assessment is more than a repeated list of facts. Show the connection between the clues and your interpretation, while leaving room for alternatives.

title: Plan: propose next steps
text: Plan describes proposed actions and follow-up. Connect each next step to the assessment and discuss it with your preceptor.
narration: A proposed action should have a reason. Consider what information you still need and explain how the next step could address that gap.

title: Put SOAP together
text: Begin with reports and findings, then explain your interpretation and proposed actions. Keep each detail in the section that reflects its role.
narration: Try following the story from evidence to judgment to action. Can your listener tell which details came from the patient and which came from your examination?

title: Why history matters
accessibleDescription: A health record is connected to medication, allergy, family, and daily-life history symbols.
text: The presenting complaint is one part of the patient's story. History adds context for clinical reasoning and a practical care plan.
narration: Before you settle on an explanation, consider what else you need to know about this person. Their prior health and daily circumstances can change how you understand the complaint.

title: Review medical history
accessibleDescription: A clinician discusses medication and allergy history with an older patient, alongside medicine and allergy symbols.
text: Ask about prior conditions, medications, allergies, and immunizations. Clarify relevant details rather than assuming a list is complete.
narration: A medication list or an allergy label is a starting point for questions. Explore what the patient takes and what reactions they describe so the history keeps its meaning.

title: Surgical and family history
accessibleDescription: A clinician asks an older patient about prior surgery and family health, with surgical and family-tree motifs.
text: Ask about prior operations and relevant family conditions. Connect these details to the current concern without assuming they explain it.
narration: Past procedures and family patterns can raise useful questions. Notice their relevance, but avoid treating a family condition as a diagnosis for this patient.

title: Understand daily life
accessibleDescription: A clinician and older patient discuss daily life, with home, work, and social-support symbols.
text: Explore substance use, occupation, living situation, environment, diet, and activity. Ask about financial security, social support, and cultural or spiritual considerations.
narration: Use open, respectful questions about daily life. Resources, support, and environmental exposures may matter, but let the patient describe their circumstances rather than filling in assumptions.

title: Put the history together
text: Select history details relevant to the complaint and proposed care. Explain how medical, family, surgical, and social context shape your understanding.
narration: You do not need to recite every detail with equal emphasis. Make the relevant connections visible, and identify any missing information you would clarify before planning care.

title: Why review systems?
accessibleDescription: A body silhouette and organ symbols represent body systems reviewed through patient-reported symptoms.
text:
The review of systems asks about patient-reported symptoms that may have been overlooked.

It adds context to the history; it is not a physical examination or a diagnostic test.
narration: Patients may not connect another symptom with their main concern. A review of systems gives them another opportunity to describe what they have experienced.

title: Use a systematic review
accessibleDescription: A clinician asks a patient about symptoms across body systems, illustrated by a body silhouette and organ symbols.
text: Ask about symptoms across body systems in an organized way. Include constitutional, respiratory, cardiovascular, and other relevant symptom areas.
narration: An organized flow helps you avoid overlooked areas. Use symptom questions the patient can understand; the purpose is a fuller history, not memorizing a system count.

title: Reports differ from findings
text: Reported shortness of breath belongs in the history. Crackles heard during an examination are objective findings.
narration: Listen for where the information came from. Asking about breathing and listening to the lungs answer different questions, even though both concern the respiratory system.

title: Connect ROS to the history
accessibleDescription: A clinician listens to reported symptoms and records the history, with symptom and timeline motifs.
text: Bring relevant reported symptoms and negatives into the clinical history. Keep them separate from examination findings as you interpret the case.
narration: Return to the patient's original concern and consider what the additional reports contribute. Record what was actually asked and reported rather than inventing reassuring negatives.

title: Examine with a purpose
accessibleDescription: A clinician performs a focused chest examination on a seated patient using a stethoscope.
text: A focused physical examination gathers targeted, observable, and measurable findings. It follows questions raised by the history.
narration: The examination gives you another source of evidence. Think about which findings could help you evaluate the possibilities raised by the patient's story.

title: Let history guide the exam
accessibleDescription: A clinician discusses a relevant chest examination with a patient, alongside a chest and lung illustration.
text: Select examination areas relevant to the patient's symptoms and possible explanations. Use an organized flow to gather the findings you need.
narration: For Mr. Jones, the chest-pain history makes respiratory and cardiac findings relevant. Explain why you would examine an area rather than choosing it from a random checklist.

title: Separate reports and measurements
text: A patient's pain description is subjective. Vital signs and observed examination findings are objective.
narration: Ask yourself who supplied each detail and how it was obtained. Keep the patient's experience visible while distinguishing it from your own observations.

title: Connect findings to reasoning
accessibleDescription: A clinician listens to an older patient’s lungs with a stethoscope, alongside lung and sound symbols marked with a check and a question.
text: Use examination findings to support or challenge diagnostic possibilities. A finding adds evidence; it does not automatically establish or exclude a diagnosis.
narration: Mr. Jones's crackles contribute to a pulmonary possibility. Consider what they explain and what they leave unresolved, including the competing cardiac concern.

title: What is a differential?
accessibleDescription: A learner considers multiple clinical possibilities represented by different body-system cards.
text: A differential diagnosis is a prioritized list of plausible explanations. It makes your working diagnosis and alternatives explicit.
narration: Clinical reasoning begins with possibilities, not certainty. A useful list helps you explain what you think is happening and what else deserves consideration.

title: Identify plausible explanations
accessibleDescription: A clinical mentor and learner discuss possible explanations, with a thought-network and evidence symbols.
text: Use the history and examination to identify possibilities. In Mr. Jones's case, consider pulmonary and cardiac explanations.
narration: Choose possibilities that connect to the supplied evidence. Avoid adding diagnoses only to make the list longer; be ready to explain why each belongs.

title: Compare the evidence
accessibleDescription: A clinician considers patient information and connected evidence symbols while forming a clinical interpretation.
text: Pain with inspiration and crackles support a pulmonary possibility. Age and hypertension keep a cardiac possibility under consideration.
narration: Compare both sides of your reasoning. A clue that favors one explanation does not erase competing evidence or safely exclude another cause.

title: Prioritize your possibilities
text: List the working diagnosis first, then relevant alternatives. Explain how supporting evidence and important unresolved concerns shape your priorities.
narration: Your order communicates your judgment. Distinguish the explanation you currently favor from alternatives that still need attention, and be ready to revise as evidence changes.

title: Communicate uncertainty
text: State what supports your interpretation and what remains unclear. Identify the question you want to discuss with your preceptor.
narration: Naming uncertainty helps your preceptor understand where you need guidance. Try a specific question about the evidence instead of presenting an unsupported conclusion.

title: Why structured handoffs matter
accessibleDescription: Why structured handoffs matter
text: SBAR organizes a concise handoff into Situation, Background, Assessment, and Recommendation. Share your judgment and a proposed next step.
narration: A busy listener needs a clear path through the case. S-bar helps you lead with the concern and finish with a request they can respond to.

title: Situation: the current concern
text: Identify the patient and the immediate concern. Mr. Jones is 65 and presents with anterior chest pain that began yesterday morning.
narration: Start with what is happening now and why you are presenting the patient. Save the supporting detail for the next part so the opening stays focused.

title: Background: relevant context
text: Give the history and findings needed to understand the concern. Include Mr. Jones's hypertension, COPD, pain pattern, and lung crackles.
narration: Select background that helps your listener interpret the situation. Keep reported symptoms and examination findings distinguishable, even in a brief presentation.

title: Assessment: your judgment
text: Explain your interpretation of the evidence. Pulmonary clues are present, while a cardiac explanation remains a concern.
narration: This is where your listener hears your thinking. Connect the evidence to your possibilities and acknowledge what the available facts cannot settle.

title: Recommendation: a proposed action
text: Propose a next step and explain its purpose. Ask your preceptor for guidance on the unresolved concern.
narration: Make your request specific enough for a response. Discuss the rationale with your preceptor; the teaching case is not a stand-alone diagnostic or treatment protocol.

title: Put SBAR together
text: Present the situation, relevant background, assessment, and recommendation in order. Close with a clear request for your preceptor's input.
narration: Listen to your own handoff as if you were receiving it. Can the preceptor identify the main concern, follow your judgment, and understand what you are asking?

title: Lead the learning conversation
accessibleDescription: Lead the learning conversation
text: SNAPPS is a learner-led presentation framework. It connects a concise case summary with reasoning, uncertainty, planning, and learning.
narration: Take an active role in the conversation rather than waiting for every question. SNAPPS gives your preceptor a window into both your reasoning and your learning needs.

title: Summarize: concise findings
accessibleDescription: Summarize: concise findings
text: Briefly present the relevant history and examination findings. Retain the details that help explain the clinical concern.
narration: A useful summary is selective without distorting the case. Ask which details your preceptor needs to understand the possibilities you will discuss next.

title: Narrow: two or three possibilities
accessibleDescription: Narrow: two or three possibilities
text: Choose two or three plausible diagnoses to discuss. Connect each possibility to the case evidence.
narration: Narrowing makes the discussion manageable. It does not mean the remaining possibilities are proven or that important alternatives can be dismissed.

title: Analyze: compare diagnoses
text: Compare supporting and conflicting evidence for your possibilities. Explain which findings distinguish them and what remains unresolved.
narration: Move beyond naming diagnoses to explaining your comparison. For Mr. Jones, describe how pulmonary clues and cardiac risk factors influence your thinking.

title: Probe: ask about uncertainty
accessibleDescription: Probe: ask about uncertainty
text: Ask your preceptor a specific question about a gap in your reasoning. Explain what you understand and where you need guidance.
narration: A focused question invites a useful teaching conversation. Name the decision or evidence you are uncertain about without treating stable vitals as proof that a concerning cause is excluded.

title: Plan: propose management
accessibleDescription: Plan: propose management
text: Propose next steps linked to your assessment. Discuss the rationale and unresolved concerns with your preceptor.
narration: Bring a reasoned proposal to the conversation and be ready to adjust it. Your preceptor can help connect the plan to the patient's needs and the uncertainty in the case.

title: Select: a learning question
accessibleDescription: Select: a learning question
text: Choose one focused, case-related question for self-directed learning. Make it specific enough to investigate and bring back to discussion.
narration: Turn a gap from this encounter into a learning task. For example, you could study how chest-pain characteristics inform a differential, then share what you learned.

title: Put SNAPPS together
text: Summarize, Narrow, Analyze, Probe, Plan, and Select. Keep the presentation concise while making your reasoning and learning needs clear.
narration: Check that your presentation includes all six moves. The goal is a collaborative conversation where your preceptor can follow your thinking and help you develop it.
